items.title: McCarthy was censured by his own Senate in 1954
items.claim: How did Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist campaign end?

options.text: After televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed his methods, the Senate voted 67-22 to censure him on 2 December 1954; he died of liver failure in 1957 aged 48
He resigned and joined the Republican Party leadership

items.reveal:
McCarthy had risen on a 1950 Wheeling speech claiming 205 communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings (April-June 1954) were televised; Army counsel Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' on 9 June became the iconic moment.

Edward R. Murrow's CBS broadcast 'See It Now' on 9 March 1954 had already turned mainstream opinion. The Senate censure vote followed in December.

HUAC (House Un-American Activities Committee), the Hollywood blacklist, loyalty oaths and the Smith Act prosecutions continued separately and outlasted McCarthy.
items.why: McCarthyism as a phenomenon was bigger than McCarthy. His fall did not end the Red Scare — but it ended one specific style of grandstanding accusation, and television was central to both his rise and fall.

items.title: The Pyramids were built by paid workers, not slaves
items.claim: Who built the Great Pyramid at Giza (c. 2560 BCE)?

options.text: Skilled Egyptian craftsmen and rotating teams of agricultural workers, housed in a workers' town with bakeries and medical care — graves of those who died on the job have been found
Forced labour from Egypt's foreign conquests only
Mercenaries paid in gold from Nubia

items.reveal_title: A workforce, not a chain gang
items.reveal:
Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass excavated the workers' town south of the Giza plateau from the 1980s. They found bakeries producing thousands of loaves daily, fish-processing areas, a medical facility and graves with healed injuries — evidence of long-term care.

Graffiti in the relieving chambers of the Great Pyramid records work-gang names ('Friends of Khufu', 'Drunkards of Menkaure'). Estimates suggest a permanent workforce of perhaps 4,000-5,000 with seasonal labour bringing it to 20,000.

The slave-building myth comes partly from Herodotus (5th century BCE, writing 2,000 years later) and partly from biblical-cinema conflation with the Exodus story.
items.why: The Pyramids as monuments to oppression is a cultural cliché. The archaeological record shows organised state labour with bread rations and beer — not chained slaves under whips.
